surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (Germany)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, fit and comfort priorities, and sustainability trade-offs.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: High-frequency runners who train for races or personal bests. They prioritize cushioning, responsiveness, and durability, and are willing to pay a premium for technology and brand reputation. They research extensively and are less price-sensitive.

segments.name: Value-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Run or walk for fitness and commuting, often on a budget. They seek durable, comfortable shoes at a reasonable price. Price increases and tariffs directly affect their choices, and they are likely to switch brands for a better deal.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Consumers
segments.description: Environmentally motivated buyers who want sustainable materials and ethical production. They are willing to pay somewhat more for eco-friendly options but still weigh price. They may run casually or use shoes for everyday wear.

segments.name: Style-Led Casual Users
segments.description: Buy running shoes primarily for fashion, lifestyle, or light recreational use. They are influenced by brand image, design, and trends. They run infrequently but buy multiple pairs. Price sensitivity is moderate.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Running Shoes buyers in Germany. It asks how people use Running Shoes, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Germany who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. Excluded: Professional athletes whose shoes are provided by sponsors; Businesses purchasing shoes for employees or resale; Children under 18 (unless purchasing for themselves, but typically parent decides).
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least occasionally
Purchases athletic footwear for fitness, sport, or casual wear
Researches brands, reviews, and features before buying
May be brand loyal or open to switching based on price/performance
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's running identity—frequency, context, and motivation—and their current shoe ownership. It then follows their purchase journey from trigger through research, channel, and spend, ending with the decision drivers. Next, it probes their specific needs and trade-offs, including fit, sustainability, and value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, frustrations, and future switching intent, providing the data to classify each respondent into one of four segments.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Running Shoes in Germany — who Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. The survey targets the end consumer who buys and uses running shoes for personal fitness and lifestyle. This audience represents the primary market for running shoes globally.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: High-frequency runners who train for races or personal bests. They prioritize cushioning, responsiveness, and durability, and are willing to pay a premium for technology and brand reputation. They research extensively and are less price-sensitive.
segments.hypothesis: This group reports the highest weekly mileage, the highest spend per pair, and the strongest preference for performance attributes over price or style.

segments.name: Value-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Run or walk for fitness and commuting, often on a budget. They seek durable, comfortable shoes at a reasonable price. Price increases and tariffs directly affect their choices, and they are likely to switch brands for a better deal.
segments.hypothesis: This group shows the highest price sensitivity, the lowest average spend, and the strongest tendency to wait for sales or choose budget brands.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Consumers
segments.description: Environmentally motivated buyers who want sustainable materials and ethical production. They are willing to pay somewhat more for eco-friendly options but still weigh price. They may run casually or use shoes for everyday wear.
segments.hypothesis: This group ranks sustainable materials as a top purchase driver and is willing to pay a moderate premium for verified eco-credentials.

segments.name: Style-Led Casual Users
segments.description: Buy running shoes primarily for fashion, lifestyle, or light recreational use. They are influenced by brand image, design, and trends. They run infrequently but buy multiple pairs. Price sensitivity is moderate.
segments.hypothesis: This group has the lowest running frequency but the highest number of pairs owned, and prioritizes style and brand over technical performance.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's running identity—frequency, context, and motivation—and their current shoe ownership. It then follows their purchase journey from trigger through research, channel, and spend, ending with the decision drivers. Next, it probes their specific needs and trade-offs, including fit, sustainability, and value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, frustrations, and future switching intent, providing the data to classify each respondent into one of four segments.
storyline_notes: Replaced generic 'category relationship' with 'running participation and frequency' to directly segment by engagement.
Added 'where and how they run' to capture context (road vs trail vs treadmill) which is critical for shoe needs.
Added 'shoe ownership' to capture number of pairs and rotation, which differentiates style-led buyers from performance runners.
Added 'fit and sizing confidence' as a distinct beat because fit is a top pain point in the market and a key differentiator.
Added 'sustainability expectations' as a beat to address the high environmental awareness in Europe.
Added 'replacement cycle' to the buying section to understand durability expectations and purchase frequency.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
